title: What if the Moon were twice as close? #shorts
description:
Halve the distance to the Moon and the physics gets wild: a 9.7-day month, tidal pull 8 times stronger, and a Moon four times bigger in the sky.

Numbers: average Earth–Moon distance 384,400 km; orbital period scales with distance^1.5 (Kepler's third law); tidal force scales with 1/distance^3.

scenes.say: What if the Moon were suddenly twice as close to Earth?

show.text: What if the Moon were twice as close?

scenes.say: Today it circles about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres away. Halve that, and everything changes.

show.label: Distance to the Moon, cut in half

scenes.say: Closer orbits are faster. A lunar month would shrink from twenty-seven days to under ten.
Tidal pull grows with the cube of closeness, so the Moon would tug on our oceans eight times harder.
Coasts would face far bigger tides twice a day, and total solar eclipses would become an ordinary event.

show.text: Bigger tides, twice a day. *Total* *eclipses,* all the time.

scenes.say: And at night, it would look four times bigger in the sky.

show.label: the Moon's size in our sky (by area)
